strengths: Compelling and practically relevant formulation: The paper effectively identifies the gap between Text-to-SQL (which lacks continuous morphological expressivity) and Time Series Question Answering (which cannot scale to long database histories), formulating the NLQ4TSDB problem clearly.

Well-motivated neuro-symbolic design: The 'Search-Then-Verify' framework (Sonar-TS) is conceptually sound and pragmatic, leveraging multi-scale SAX and summary statistics in SQL for high-recall candidate pruning, followed by precise Python-based algorithmic verification (PELT, DTW, ACF).

Comprehensive benchmark construction: NLQTSBench provides a structured 4-level taxonomy across 831 queries with rigorous evaluation metrics (IoU, Set-F1, composite report scoring), balancing real-world background telemetry with auditable ground truth via controlled injection and human validation.

Strong empirical validation and insightful ablations: The experimental results substantially outperform existing Text-to-SQL and time-series foundation model baselines. The ablation study clearly highlights the necessity of feature tables, domain experiences, and Python verification.
weaknesses: Baseline comparability: The comparison against standard Text-to-SQL baselines (e.g., MAC-SQL, Xiyan-SQL) is somewhat asymmetric because these baselines only output SQL queries without access to the external Python verification library. Including a generic code-agent baseline (e.g., ReAct/Code-LLM equipped with the same Python tools but querying raw data directly) would better isolate the precise benefit of the SQL/SAX indexing stage.

Domain diversity of NLQTSBench: The benchmark is constructed primarily on top of a single base dataset (CausalRivers) with synthetic pattern injections for Levels 2–4. Evaluating or discussing generalizability across more heterogeneous real-world domains (e.g., high-frequency financial data, cloud server telemetry, or medical biosignals) would further strengthen the claims.

Lack of latency and computational cost analysis: While the motivation emphasizes computational feasibility and pruning efficiency over massive histories, the empirical evaluation lacks quantitative runtime metrics (e.g., query execution latency, database I/O overhead, and indexing cost) compared to direct Python scans.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated problem formulation: The paper identifies a crucial blind spot at the intersection of relational Text-to-SQL (which lacks continuous morphological expressivity) and Time Series Question Answering (which suffers from severe context-length bottlenecks over TSDB-scale histories).

Pragmatic and elegant neuro-symbolic framework: Decoupling the pipeline into coarse SQL-based candidate localization via multi-scale symbolic indices (SAX) and fine-grained verification via domain-specific Python algorithmic primitives (PELT, DTW, ACF) is an intuitive, practical, and effective design.

Comprehensive benchmark design: NLQTSBench introduces a structured four-level taxonomy (from basic numerical retrieval to multi-stage narrative report generation) with 831 verified queries over long-horizon temporal contexts, backed by automated quality checks and human verification.

Thorough empirical evaluation and ablation: The experiments systematically evaluate performance across short-context and long-history regimes, accompanied by clear ablation studies demonstrating the distinct contributions of the multi-scale feature tables, experience memory, and Python verification engine.
weaknesses: Lack of a general Code-Interpreter / LLM Agent baseline: The Text-to-SQL baselines (MAC-SQL, Xiyan-SQL, Omini-SQL) generate pure SQL and lack the algorithmic execution capabilities of Python, making their failure on complex morphological tasks almost guaranteed. A critical missing baseline is a standard LLM Code-Interpreter/ReAct agent equipped with SQL and general Python execution (without the SAX indexing and Sonar-TS framework) to isolate the performance gain of the proposed Search-Then-Verify indexing strategy versus mere code execution.

Potential bias from synthetic injection: Tasks in Levels 2–4 rely on mathematically defined pattern injection (Gaussian spikes, dual-Sigmoid shifts, composite sinusoids) on top of CausalRivers backgrounds. While this provides verifiable ground truth, it also closely aligns with the mathematical primitives in the verification operator library, which may overstate real-world performance on messy, unmodeled industrial anomalies.

Unclear train/val/test split regarding Experience accumulation: Section 4.3.2 and Appendix B.2 detail an evolving experience memory via closed-loop reflection. It is unclear whether these experiences were collected on a disjoint training split of queries or accumulated across the evaluation set, raising potential concerns regarding test-set contamination or evaluation protocol consistency.

Missing latency, storage, and scalability profiling: A core premise of using feature tables and TSDBs is computational feasibility. However, the manuscript lacks quantitative runtime measurements (query latency, end-to-end execution time, and index storage overhead relative to raw data) across varying data scales.

strengths: Compelling and practical problem formulation: Bridging natural language querying and Time Series Databases (NLQ4TSDB) addresses a prominent gap between relational Text-to-SQL (which cannot capture morphological time series semantics) and end-to-end TS foundation models (which are constrained by context windows).

Comprehensive benchmark design: NLQTSBench introduces a four-level hierarchical taxonomy (Basic Operations, Pattern Recognition, Semantic Reasoning, Insight Synthesis) with 831 queries over realistic background signals (CausalRivers), backed by verifiable injection, human auditing, and rigorous evaluation metrics (e.g., IoU, composite report score).

Sound neuro-symbolic system architecture: The 'Search-Then-Verify' pipeline cleanly decouples coarse symbolic filtering via multi-scale SAX indexing in SQL from fine-grained Python verification using specialized time series primitives (PELT, DTW, Theil-Sen), supported by an iterative prompt cold-start learning loop.

Thorough ablation and presentation: The manuscript is well-structured and clearly isolates the empirical value of the feature index, the experience distillation mechanism, and the verification step across various analytical tasks.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison on the primary benchmark: On the default long-history NLQTSBench, Sonar-TS is compared exclusively against standard Text-to-SQL frameworks (MAC-SQL, Xiyan-SQL, Omini-SQL). These baselines are strictly constrained to generating SQL statements and lack access to Python execution or the domain-specific time series algorithmic library (e.g., PELT, DTW). It is unsurprising that standard SQL fails on tasks like changepoint detection or subsequence matching. A critical missing baseline is a general LLM-based Code/Data Agent (e.g., a Code-Interpreter / ReAct agent with Python access and standard time-series packages) operating over the database.

Discrepancy in model capacity across Lite baselines: For NLQTSBench-Lite, Sonar-TS employs DeepSeek-V3 as its backbone alongside its verification operator suite, whereas the compared time series models (ChatTS-14B, ITFormer-7B, Time-R1) are substantially smaller and fundamentally different in architecture, making it difficult to disentangle the benefits of the workflow from the sheer reasoning capacity of a frontier LLM.

Lack of analysis on indexing storage and update overhead: Sonar-TS relies on offline materialization of multi-scale feature tables (Daily, Monthly, Yearly) and SAX strings. In production TSDB environments characterized by high write/ingestion rates and thousands of channels, materializing and maintaining multi-granular SAX indices can introduce significant storage and latency overhead. The paper lacks experimental evaluation of indexing build time, storage amplification, and maintainability under streaming writes.

Potential bias and synthetic artifacts in data generation: The morphological queries in Levels 2–4 are synthesized by injecting idealized parametric mathematical functions (Gaussian kernels, sigmoids, sinusoids) into stationary background windows. This controlled setup may overfit the assumptions of SAX string patterns and standard algorithmic detectors (e.g., PELT and ACF), which often struggle on uncurated real-world industrial series with non-stationary noise, missing values, and irregular sampling.

Underspecified train/test protocol for Experience distillation: The prompt cold-start mechanism distills execution trajectories into high-level rules. The paper does not clearly specify the split or set of queries used to accumulate these experiences, leaving open questions regarding out-of-domain generalization and potential test-set leakage in the injected experience pool.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically significant problem: bridging the gap between natural language querying and massive time series databases (NLQ4TSDB), where standard Text-to-SQL lacks morphological expressivity and neural TSQA models fail to scale to ultra-long horizons.

Proposes a sound and pragmatic neuro-symbolic architecture ('Search-Then-Verify') that uses multi-scale discrete symbolic indices (SAX and statistical aggregates) for fast SQL pruning, coupled with exact Python operator verification on candidate slices.

Introduces NLQTSBench, a comprehensive benchmark featuring a structured 4-level taxonomy across varied temporal scales, constructed with controlled SNR-calibrated signal injection onto real backgrounds and verified by human annotators.

Provides extensive experimental validation, including comparisons against both Text-to-SQL and foundation time series QA models, thorough component ablations, sensitivity analyses across backbone sizes and alphabet dimensions, and system runtime overheads.
weaknesses: The benchmark queries and injected ground truths rely on parameterized templates and synthetic signal injection, which may limit the diversity and linguistic messiness of real-world operational user queries.

First-stage retrieval recall remains moderate (Table 10 shows recall around 47% to 55%), indicating that the SAX-based regex filtering discards roughly half of true candidate windows before verification can even run.

The framework relies heavily on a curated set of algorithmic primitives (e.g., PELT, DTW, Theil-Sen) and a static experience prompt cache; query intents that fall outside these pre-implemented verification primitives or beyond the 20-item prompt capacity may not generalize gracefully.

The paper lacks an evaluation of the system under continuous real-time data ingestion scenarios, where materializing and updating multi-scale feature tables could introduce pipeline latency and storage overhead in high-throughput TSDBs.

strengths: Compelling problem formulation: The paper clearly identifies and formalizes the Natural Language Querying for Time Series Databases (NLQ4TSDB) problem, bridging a significant gap between Text-to-SQL (which cannot natively express continuous morphological patterns) and end-to-end TSQA models (which are bottlenecked by context windows and cannot scale to massive databases).

Principled and practical system design: The proposed 'Search-Then-Verify' neuro-symbolic paradigm is intuitive and technically sound. Using multi-scale symbolic indices (SAX) in SQL for fast candidate window pruning, followed by programmatic Python verification via specialized time-series operators, offers a scalable solution to the morphological representation gap.

Comprehensive benchmark: NLQTSBench provides a structured four-level taxonomy (basic ops, pattern recognition, semantic reasoning, insight synthesis) with 1,153 queries. The dataset generation pipeline—combining mathematical primitive injection with SNR calibration against real background series and human verification—ensures rigorous and auditable evaluation.

Thorough empirical evaluation: The paper demonstrates substantial performance gains over both leading Text-to-SQL systems and multimodal time-series foundation models. Ablation experiments clearly dissect the contribution of each component (feature tables, experiences, verification, self-correction), complemented by sensitivity analyses on SAX parameters and model backbones as well as runtime/storage overhead profiling.
weaknesses: Synthetic pattern injection bias: While synthetic injection of mathematical primitives (Gaussian pulses, dual-sigmoids) is necessary to obtain ground-truth boundaries, real-world time series patterns are often much noisier, irregular, and less cleanly separable from baseline drift, which may affect out-of-distribution real-world robustness.

Recall bottleneck in the Search stage: As shown in Table 10, the intermediate recall of the coarse SAX-based search is relatively low (~54.8% for Shape Identification and ~47.1% for Composite Trend). Because verification can only operate on retrieved candidates, missing roughly half the candidates during the regex search represents an upper bound on end-to-end recall.

Static and capped experience injection: The Prompt Cold Start mechanism relies on a static pool capped at 20 heuristics distilled from 110 hold-out instances. While effective for this benchmark, this static injection into the prompt may not easily scale across broader enterprise domains or diverse custom operator libraries without a dynamic retrieval-augmented mechanism.

Baseline comparisons could include a pure Python/agentic sliding-window baseline: The Text-to-SQL models lack any time-series operators and are naturally ill-suited for morphology tasks, while TS models cannot handle long horizons. While Table 5 includes an ablation 'w/o Feature Tables' (which resembles a generic SQL+Python agent), discussing or formalizing a standard code-interpreter agent baseline on sampled data would further clarify the exact performance-efficiency trade-off.

strengths: Compelling problem formulation: The paper clearly identifies and formalizes a significant practical problem (NLQ4TSDB) at the intersection of database systems and time series analysis, convincingly articulating why pure Text-to-SQL (lacks morphological expressivity) and pure Time Series QA models (severely bounded by context windows) fail on massive temporal databases.

Sound neuro-symbolic framework: The 'Search-Then-Verify' design pattern in Sonar-TS—using multi-scale feature tables with SAX discretization for coarse SQL-based pruning, followed by code-generated verification using formal time-series algorithms (e.g., PELT, DTW, Theil-Sen)—is technically sound, practical, and decoupled from raw sequence length O(N).

Comprehensive benchmark design: NLQTSBench addresses a critical gap in literature by offering a 4-level hierarchical evaluation taxonomy (Basic Operations, Pattern Recognition, Semantic Reasoning, Insight Synthesis) evaluated over realistic long-horizon search contexts (~12k points), alongside a 512-point Lite benchmark to enable fair comparison with context-bounded neural baselines.

Rigorous empirical evaluation and ablation: The experiments systematically evaluate representatives from both Text-to-SQL and TSQA paradigms. The ablation studies clearly isolate the impact of individual modules (feature tables, experiences, verification, self-correction), accompanied by overhead, sensitivity, and intermediate recall analysis.

Exemplary presentation and transparency: The manuscript is exceptionally well-structured and clearly written, providing complete prompts, schema definitions, complexity analysis, and a frank discussion of current limitations in the appendix.
weaknesses: Reliance on synthetic pattern injection: While real backgrounds (CausalRivers, ETTm1, SMD) and SNR calibration are used, the target patterns and queries are generated via parametric mathematical primitives (Gaussian kernels, sigmoids, sinusoids) and controlled templates. Real-world user queries and temporal patterns exhibit messier morphology and semantic nuances that may not match these synthetic forms.

Candidate retrieval recall ceiling: Table 10 reveals that the initial SQL-based search stage achieves only 54.8% recall on Shape Identification and 47.1% on Composite Trend. While candidate filtering dramatically cuts down data volume, missing nearly half the relevant windows at the search stage imposes a hard upper bound on downstream verification accuracy.

Inherent rigidity of SAX tokenization: Discretizing continuous waveforms into fixed-window SAX tokens with a 5-symbol alphabet is prone to boundary effects and temporal phase alignment issues, which likely explains why the regex matching misses candidates on short or shifted patterns.

Baseline asymmetry: General Text-to-SQL baselines (e.g., Xiyan-SQL, Omni-SQL) are evaluated without access to precomputed feature tables or the specialized time-series Python verification operators available to Sonar-TS, making their failure on morphological queries inevitable by construction.
